items.title: Containers vs VMs
items.context: A container is an isolated process sharing the host's kernel, isolated with namespaces (PID, network, mount…) and limited with cgroups (CPU, memory). A VM runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor. Containers start in milliseconds and are lighter, but isolation is weaker.

questions.prompt: What do containers on one host share?
questions.explanation: That's why a Linux container needs a Linux kernel (Docker Desktop runs a small Linux VM on Mac/Windows).

items.title: Layer caching
items.context: Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer, and a changed layer invalidates every layer after it. Copy the dependency manifest and install dependencies before copying the source code, so editing code doesn't reinstall everything.

questions.prompt: Which order rebuilds fastest after a code change?
choices: RUN npm ci → COPY package*.json → COPY . .
COPY package*.json → RUN npm ci → COPY . .
questions.explanation: The npm ci layer stays cached until package*.json changes.

items.title: Multi-stage builds
items.context: A multi-stage Dockerfile builds in one stage (with compilers, the JDK, dev dependencies) and copies only the output into a slim runtime stage (FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre, distroless…). The final image is smaller and carries fewer vulnerabilities.

questions.prompt: The main benefit of a multi-stage build is:
choices: Running several apps in one container
A small runtime image without build tools

items.title: ENTRYPOINT vs CMD
items.context: ENTRYPOINT sets the executable; CMD gives default arguments (or a default command if there's no ENTRYPOINT). Arguments after the image name in docker run replace CMD but not ENTRYPOINT.

questions.prompt: With ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"] and CMD ["--port=8080"], what runs for docker run img --port=9000 ?
questions.explanation: Run-time args replace CMD and are appended to ENTRYPOINT.

items.title: Publishing ports
items.context: EXPOSE only documents which port the app listens on. -p 8080:80 actually publishes it: host port 8080 forwards to container port 80.

questions.prompt: With docker run -p 8080:80 nginx, you open the site at:
questions.explanation: host:container — the left side is on your machine.

items.title: Persistent data
items.context: Writes inside a container land in its writable layer, which disappears when the container is removed. Named volumes (managed by Docker) or bind mounts (a host directory) keep data beyond the container's life — required for databases.

questions.prompt: You run Postgres in a container without a volume and then remove the container. The data is:

items.title: Container networking
items.context: Containers on the same user-defined bridge network (and Compose services) can reach each other by container or service name through Docker's embedded DNS. On the default bridge network, name resolution isn't provided.

questions.prompt: In docker-compose, the api service should reach the db service at:
questions.explanation: Inside the api container, localhost is the api container itself.

items.title: PID 1 and signals
items.context: The shell form CMD java -jar app.jar runs under /bin/sh -c, so the shell is PID 1 and may not forward SIGTERM to Java. The exec form CMD ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"] makes Java PID 1, so it receives SIGTERM and can shut down gracefully.

questions.prompt: docker stop always takes 10 s and the app never runs its shutdown hooks. Likely fix:
choices: Use exec-form CMD/ENTRYPOINT so the app is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM
questions.explanation: Otherwise Docker sends SIGKILL after the 10 s grace period.

items.title: Image hygiene
items.context: Use .dockerignore to keep .git, node_modules, local env files and secrets out of the build context. Add a USER directive so the process doesn't run as root. Pin versions or digests: :latest is just a tag name, not a guarantee of freshness or stability.

choices: Nothing special — it's just the default tag name
questions.explanation: Pin explicit tags (or digests) for reproducible deploys.

items.title: depends_on and readiness
items.context: In Compose, depends_on only orders container start-up; it doesn't wait for the dependency to be ready. Add a healthcheck to the db service and use depends_on: { db: { condition: service_healthy } }, or make the app retry its connections.

questions.prompt: The api container crashes because Postgres isn't ready yet, despite depends_on: [db]. Fix:
choices: Add sleep 5 before docker compose up
Add a db healthcheck and depends_on condition: service_healthy (and retries in the app)
questions.explanation: Starting isn't the same as ready to accept connections.

items.title: HEALTHCHECK
items.context: HEALTHCHECK CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1 lets Docker mark a container healthy or unhealthy. Compose and Swarm use it; Kubernetes ignores it and uses its own probes.

questions.prompt: Does Kubernetes use a Dockerfile's HEALTHCHECK?
choices: No — Kubernetes uses liveness and readiness probes instead
questions.explanation: Define probes in the Pod spec.

items.title: Debugging containers
items.context: docker logs -f <c> follows a container's stdout/stderr; docker exec -it <c> sh opens a shell inside a running container; docker inspect shows its config, network and mounts.

questions.prompt: To open a shell inside a running container:
questions.explanation: docker run would start a new container instead.

items.title: ARG vs ENV
items.context: ARG values exist only at build time (docker build --build-arg VERSION=1.2). ENV values are baked into the image and visible to the running container. Neither is safe for secrets: they show up in the image history.

questions.prompt: Which is available to the running container by default?
questions.explanation: Copy an ARG into an ENV if the app needs it at run time.

items.title: Secrets in builds
items.context: Every layer keeps its files and metadata: deleting a secret in a later RUN still leaves it in an earlier layer, and ENV/ARG values appear in docker history. Use BuildKit secret mounts (RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc …) and inject runtime secrets via the orchestrator.

questions.prompt: A Dockerfile does COPY .npmrc, then RUN npm ci && rm .npmrc. Is the token safe?
choices: Only if the token is short
No — it still exists in the COPY layer; use a BuildKit secret mount
Yes, if the image is private
questions.explanation: Anyone who can pull the image can extract the layer.

items.title: Restart policies
items.context: --restart no (the default), on-failure[:N], always, or unless-stopped (like always, but not after you stop it manually). Orchestrators replace this with their own supervision.

questions.prompt: Restart after crashes and host reboots, but not after you manually stop it:
questions.explanation: always would also bring back a container you stopped on purpose, after a daemon restart.

items.title: Tag and push
items.context: docker build -t registry.example.com/team/api:1.4.2 . names the image for a registry; docker push uploads it (after docker login). The same image can carry several tags, e.g. a version and the git SHA.

questions.prompt: Before pushing to a private registry, the image name must:
choices: Include the registry hostname, e.g. registry.example.com/team/api:1.4.2
questions.explanation: Without a hostname, Docker assumes Docker Hub.

items.title: Resource limits
items.context: docker run --memory 512m --cpus 1.5 caps a container using cgroups. Hitting the memory limit gets the process OOM-killed; CPU limits throttle it. JVMs since Java 10 read container limits for heap sizing.

questions.prompt: A container with --memory 256m tries to use 400 MB. Result:
choices: It's slowed down but keeps running
questions.explanation: Set limits, and size the app (heap, workers) to fit inside them.

items.title: Cleaning up
items.context: Unused images, stopped containers and build cache pile up. docker system df shows usage; docker system prune removes stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images and build cache (-a also removes all unused images, --volumes also removes unused volumes).

questions.prompt: A CI runner's disk fills with old images. Safe routine cleanup:
questions.explanation: Never delete Docker's data directory by hand while the daemon is running.
